name: Calcium-D-glucarate

lead: Calcium-D-glucarate is the calcium salt of glucaric acid, a sugar acid found in fruits and vegetables. Men on hormone regimens or wanting less estrogenic effect take it hoping the body clears estrogen faster, for a leaner, less soft look.

The proposed chain is that it yields D-glucaro-1,4-lactone, which inhibits beta-glucuronidase, an enzyme that can let estrogens be reabsorbed instead of excreted. Most supporting research is rodent work starting in the 1980s, often in cancer-prevention models, such as a 1997 rat study tracking the lactone after dosing.

paras: It is taken as a capsule supplement, usually as part of a broader estrogen-management routine alongside diet and training. Users typically run it for weeks to months and judge by bloodwork and how they look.

An AI-generated source describes it as generally well tolerated, with mild digestive upset, and says pregnancy and breastfeeding are contraindicated and that it may speed clearance of drugs removed by glucuronidation. That description is unverified, and no regulatory warnings were found.

angle.text: Calcium-D-glucarate is taken to help the body clear estrogen, so estrogenic effects ease and the physique looks leaner. It works, in theory, by blocking an enzyme that recycles estrogen. Most supporting studies are in rodents.

lead: Calcium D-glucarate is a salt of glucaric acid (saccharic acid), a sugar acid that occurs naturally in small amounts in mammals and in fruits and vegetables, particularly oranges, apples, grapefruit and cruciferous vegetables [1][2]. Glucarate salts are used in dietary supplements as precursors to D-glucaro-1,4-lactone, described as an inhibitor of the enzyme beta-glucuronidase [1].

In bodybuilding and hormone-management circles it is taken for its proposed effect on estrogen clearance, usually alongside diindolylmethane (DIM), fibre and liver-support products, with the aim of a leaner, less water-retentive physique [3][4][5]. The scientific literature on it consists mainly of rodent studies of chemical carcinogenesis beginning in the 1980s, in which dietary glucarate reduced tumour development, plus a 2002 review that lists estrogen metabolism and lipid lowering as potential clinical applications [6][7][2].
No clinical studies of calcium D-glucarate for appearance outcomes have been published. Wikipedia notes that more clinical research is needed to confirm health effects in humans [1].

paras: On T Nation, calcium-D-glucarate comes up as an estrogen-management supplement. One poster describes taking it to help rid the body of 'bad' estrogens, suggesting this would help lean the legs [3]. Another says DIM and calcium-D-glucarate are the two he takes, plus fibre and a liver-support formula [4]. A third says he takes both it and DIM while discussing prohormones [8], and another poster reports being advised by a coach to add a DIM product and an upcoming calcium-D-glucarate product to a body-composition program [9].

Some users describe temporary results: one wrote that two months of DIM, calcium-D-glucarate and fibre worked well at first for stubborn leg fat, then stopped, with the fat returning after he stopped [5]. A user writing about adrenal and hormone problems says he was suspicious that it might reduce SHBG further through estrogen depletion [10]. One long diet thread lists it among the ingredients of a multi-component supplement [11].

In an anastrozole thread, a poster pasted figures attributed to Dave Asprey, founder of Bulletproof Coffee, that calcium-D-glucarate cut estrogen receptors by 48 percent and serum estrogen by 23 percent in one study [12]. The thread does not cite a published study for those figures.

In the liver, many compounds, including estrogens, are conjugated to glucuronic acid for excretion. Gut bacteria produce beta-glucuronidase, which can cleave that conjugate and allow reabsorption. Proponents say that inhibiting this enzyme with glucaro-1,4-lactone increases elimination [13][2]. A 2002 review in Alternative Medicine Review states that oral calcium-D-glucarate inhibits beta-glucuronidase, an enzyme produced by colonic microflora, and that elevated activity is associated with higher risk of hormone-dependent cancers [2].

A rat study reported that D-glucaro-1,4-lactone forms in vivo after oral dosing of a glucarate salt and tracked its uptake by organs and excretion [14]. A 1986 study using serum beta-glucuronidase activity as a marker found that dietary calcium glucarate acted as a slow-release source of the lactone in rats [6].

In a 1986 rat model of chemically induced mammary tumours, a calcium glucarate-supplemented diet given after the carcinogen was reported to inhibit tumour development by more than 70 percent [6]. A second 1986 mouse study found that serum beta-glucuronidase activity differed between strains, correlated with urinary 17-ketosteroid excretion, a marker of androgen level, and that dietary calcium glucarate lowered both in susceptible strains [7]. Later animal studies covered colon tumours in rats given potassium hydrogen glucarate [15], skin tumours in mice given glucarate with other phytochemicals [16], apoptosis in carcinogen-exposed mouse skin [17] and inflammatory markers in a mouse lung tumour model [18]. A laboratory comparison in human blood platelets examined antioxidant activity of calcium-D-glucarate and related glucose derivatives [19]. Review literature discusses glucarate among agents examined for cancer prevention [20].

For context, Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports a placebo-controlled trial of 68 women using a combination product that included calcium D-glucarate, and describes human evidence as limited, with no large phase 3 trials or meta-analyses [13]. That description is not independently verified here.

Grokipedia states that the supplement is generally well tolerated, that it is not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding because of insufficient data, and that it may increase clearance of drugs eliminated by glucuronidation [13]. The Wikipedia article on glucaric acid gives hazard data only for the pure chemical, not for supplement use [1]. A forum user raised the question whether lowering estrogen too far could affect SHBG, which is the user's own concern rather than a published finding [10].

Physique communities group calcium-D-glucarate with other estrogen-management measures: DIM and cruciferous-vegetable extracts, dietary fibre, green tea and liver-support supplements, as well as prescription aromatase inhibitors and the other drugs discussed in threads on anastrozole [4][3][12].

lore.intro: On T Nation, calcium-D-glucarate is mentioned as an estrogen-clearing supplement, often with DIM, by people dieting, using hormones or prohormones, or discussing estrogen-related fat [3][8][4].
